transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I… I came in because I’m scared of where my thoughts have been going. I keep thinking it would be better if I just didn’t wake up. Like if I could just go to sleep and not have to open my eyes again, that would be easier for everybody.

And it’s not just being tired, you know? It feels heavier than that. Sometimes I get this feeling like dying would be the fair punishment for what I’ve done to my family and my crew. Like I’ve caused too much damage or let people down too badly, and there should be some kind of consequence for that. I know that probably sounds awful to say out loud, but it’s been in my head a lot, and I didn’t know what else to do.
Did something traumatic happen before these thoughts started?

I don’t know if I’d call it traumatic exactly, but… my husband got injured, and a few months after that is when this really settled in. It wasn’t like one single day where everything changed, at least not for me emotionally. It was more like things kept piling up, and then a few months later I realized I wasn’t coming back up out of it.

So… the depression, this heaviness, has been with me for about a year and two months now. I keep thinking back and trying to pinpoint it, because I know people ask, like, “When did it start?” And the best I can say is it started a few months after his injury and it just… stayed. It didn’t lift the way I thought it might.
Before this past year, was there ever another time in your life when you went through a period like this depression?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I’ve had hard times before, everybody has, and I’ve been sad or stressed before. Work stuff, family stuff, money stuff, the usual things that can wear you down.

But if you mean like this — where it just stays and everything feels this heavy for this long — I don’t know. I don’t think I can point to another time that was exactly like this. I’ve been trying to think back, but it’s kind of blurry, because at the time you don’t always label it as “a period” or anything. You just keep getting up and doing what you have to do.

This past year feels different to me, though. It’s like it took root and didn’t let up. Before that, I guess I had low points, but I can’t really say there was another stretch that was the same as this.
When your husband was injured, did you witness it happen?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t really have a clear memory of seeing the actual moment it happened, if that’s what you mean. Like, I know he was injured, and I know what happened around it, and I’ve gone over it in my head so many times that sometimes it almost feels like I can picture pieces of it, but I don’t want to say I witnessed it if I didn’t actually see it with my own eyes.

It’s kind of all tangled together now — what I was told, what I imagined, what I remember from afterward. So… no, I don’t think I can say I witnessed the injury happen directly. At least not in a way I’m confident about.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually high, energized, or like you needed much less sleep than usual?

I don’t really know. I mean, I understand what you’re asking, I think — like feeling wired or on top of the world, or not needing sleep and still having all this energy — but I can’t clearly point to a time like that.

There have been times I’ve stayed up late because I couldn’t settle, or because my mind wouldn’t shut off, but that doesn’t feel like what you’re describing exactly. It’s not like I was energized in a good way or suddenly doing a million things and feeling amazing. At least, not that I can remember.

I guess I’d say I haven’t noticed anything like being unusually high or needing much less sleep in that way. But I’m also second-guessing myself, because sometimes when you ask it like that, I start wondering, “Well, what counts as unusual?” But no, nothing really stands out to me like that.
Do you have unwanted memories or nightmares about your husband’s injury that keep coming back?

I don’t know if I’d call them memories exactly. That’s part of what gets confusing for me. I do think about it sometimes, and it can come up when I don’t really want it to, but I’m not sure it’s like a flashback or anything like that. It’s more like my mind circles around it, and then I start questioning what I actually remember versus what I’ve filled in.

As far as nightmares… I can’t really say I have clear nightmares about the injury itself. I mean, I’ve had bad dreams before, but I don’t wake up thinking, “That was the accident,” or seeing it all over again in some exact way. At least not that I can clearly identify.

So… I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure. I don’t think I have unwanted memories or nightmares about it in the way you might be asking, but it does sit in my head sometimes, if that makes sense.
Before this past year, was there ever a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. Before this past year… I mean, I’ve had low periods, sure, but when you say depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks, I start trying to measure it like, “Was it every day? Was it two full weeks? Was I just stressed or tired?” And then I get kind of stuck.

I don’t have a clear memory of a specific stretch where I can say, yes, that was definitely two weeks straight of being depressed nearly every day. It may have happened in some way, but I don’t want to say yes if I’m just filling in the blanks.

So I guess my answer is… I don’t know. Nothing specific is coming to mind from before this past year that I can confidently point to.
Is the stress from your husband’s injury still going on in your life now?

Yes. It’s still going on. It’s been… about a year and five months now, I think, since my husband hurt his back and became mostly stuck at home. I don’t know, sometimes I lose track because it all kind of blends together, but it’s definitely not over.

It’s not like it was just an accident and then things went back to normal. His injury changed the way things run every day, and that stress is still just part of the house now. So yes, it’s ongoing — it’s been going on since then.
When you have a day that feels a little lighter, is it usually because something about your husband’s situation eases up?

I’m not sure I can connect it that directly. I mean… sometimes if something with him is calmer that day, maybe the house feels a little less tight, if that makes sense. But I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear pattern where I think, “Oh, today feels lighter because his situation eased up.”

Some days feel a little better and I can’t really tell why. It might be the mood in the house, or maybe I slept differently, or maybe I just got through the morning without as much pressure building up. And other days, even if nothing new is happening with him, I still feel weighed down by it, like it’s just there in the background.

So I guess… maybe sometimes, but I wouldn’t want to say that’s usually the reason. I haven’t really tracked it that closely.
When something genuinely good happens, does your mood lift, even briefly?

I’m not completely sure. I mean, I think it depends what you mean by “lift.” If something good happens, I can recognize that it’s good, like I know I should feel glad about it, and sometimes there is a little… I don’t know, a little break in the heaviness maybe.

But I don’t know if I’d call it my whole mood lifting. Sometimes it’s more like I smile or I say, “That’s good,” but inside it still feels kind of flat or weighed down. Other times maybe I do feel lighter for a short bit, but then it fades pretty fast and I’m back to the same place.

So I guess my honest answer is maybe briefly sometimes, but I haven’t really paid close enough attention to say it clearly. It’s not like I reliably bounce up when something good happens.
Even on days when nothing stressful is happening with your husband, do you still feel depressed?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I wish I could say it only happens when something with him is bad that day, because then at least it would make sense, like there’s a direct reason right in front of me. But even on days when there isn’t some new crisis or he’s not needing as much or the house is quieter, I still feel it.

For most of the time since all this started, it’s just been there. The guilt is there, like I’m failing somehow or not doing enough. The exhaustion is there even when the day itself isn’t especially stressful. I still don’t really feel interested in things the way I used to, even if there’s technically time or space to do something. And… the thoughts about death, those have been there too. Not every single second, and some weeks are less crushing than others, but they don’t just disappear because that particular day is calmer.

So yes, even when nothing big is happening with my husband, I still feel depressed. It’s more like the stress made everything worse, but the depression doesn’t turn off just because the stress is quiet for a little while.
Do you believe you truly deserve to die as punishment for what you’ve done?

I… that’s hard to say out loud. Part of me knows, or at least I’m supposed to know, that nobody should be thinking of death as some kind of punishment. But when I’m really down in it, yes, it feels like that. It feels like maybe it would be fair, like if I didn’t wake up, that would be what I deserve for what I’ve done to my family and my crew.

That’s actually part of why I came in, because those thoughts keep coming back. It’s not just “I’m tired” in a normal way. It’s more like I keep thinking it would be better if I didn’t wake up, like everyone would be spared me or the damage I’ve caused. And then I feel ashamed even saying that, because I know how awful that sounds.

I don’t know if I believe it every minute, but when the guilt gets really loud, dying feels like the punishment that would match it. Like that would settle the account somehow. And I know that probably doesn’t make sense from the outside, but inside it can feel very real.
Before this past year, was there ever a time when you lost interest or pleasure in most things for at least two weeks?

Before this past year… no, not like this. I mean, I’ve had tired stretches before, like anybody, where I didn’t feel like doing much for a few days, or I’d skip something because work ran me into the ground. But I still had things that felt like mine.

I used to paint. Not professionally or anything, but I’d get lost in it for hours. And I liked cooking big meals, especially if people were coming over or even just making too much food because it felt good to make something. I used to run before jobs sometimes, even if it was early and I complained about it, because it cleared my head. And theater rehearsals… I’d show up for those. I cared about being there, about the lines and the people and the whole thing.

Now all of that feels like chores from somebody else’s life. Like I can remember that I used to care, but I don’t feel connected to it. If I miss rehearsal or don’t paint or don’t cook, there’s not even much disappointment, just this blankness, like, “Okay, I didn’t do it.” So before this past year, I don’t think I had a two-week period where most things lost their pleasure like that. This feels different.
Do you believe you actually caused your husband’s injury?

I… I don’t know how to answer that in a clean way. If you mean, do I know for a fact that I directly caused it, like with my own hands or because I chose one exact thing that made it happen… I don’t know. I can’t prove that. But inside, it feels like yes. It feels like I’m the reason he got worse.

I keep going back over everything, every decision, every job, every time I pushed or didn’t push, every time I was distracted or tired or thought something would be fine. And it all turns into this one conclusion in my head, that if I had been different, better, more careful, less selfish, then maybe he wouldn’t have gotten hurt or maybe he wouldn’t have gotten worse after. It’s like I infected the whole situation somehow.

And it’s not just him. I keep thinking the crew lost work because of me, and the clients’ homes got messed up because of me, and everything I touched turned bad. Like I poisoned it. That’s the phrase that keeps coming up in my head, like I poisoned everything I touched. So when you ask if I believe I caused his injury… I guess I believe I caused the damage around it, even if I can’t explain it in a way that would make sense to someone else.

And then it feels like whatever happens to me after that, I deserve it. Like if people are angry, if things fall apart, if I lose everything, that’s just the consequence of what I did. It feels hard to separate what actually happened from what I feel responsible for, because the guilt just swallows the whole thing.
Do you believe, as a fact, that you poisoned everything you touched?

As a fact… I mean, I know how that sounds. If you’re asking me like, could someone test it or prove it, no, I don’t think there’s some literal poison on my hands or anything like that. I know that doesn’t make sense in that kind of way.

But it feels true. That’s the problem. It feels like everything I was near got ruined because of me. My husband got worse, and I keep thinking there had to be something I did or didn’t do that made that happen. The crew lost work, and I hear myself saying, “That’s because of me.” Clients’ homes got messed up, and even if there are a hundred other reasons something went wrong, my mind goes straight to, “You touched it, you were involved, so of course it went bad.”

So do I believe it as a fact? I don’t know. Maybe not in the way you mean “fact.” But when I’m sitting alone with it, it doesn’t feel like just a thought. It feels like the truth about me, like I damage things by being part of them. And then whatever happens to me after that feels deserved. Like if everything falls apart, that’s just what should happen because I caused it.
Has anyone else told you that you are not actually to blame for what happened, but you still feel completely certain that you are?

Yes. People have said that to me. My husband has, in his way, and other people too, like they’ll say, “You couldn’t have known,” or “That wasn’t on you,” or “There were other reasons things went wrong.” They try to explain it like it was circumstances, or bad luck, or decisions other people made, not something I caused.

And I hear them. I can repeat the words back. I understand, in my head, what they’re trying to tell me. But it doesn’t land. It’s like there’s this wall between what they say and what I feel is true.

Because I still keep coming back to the same thing: my husband got worse, the crew lost work, clients’ homes got messed up, and I was right there in the middle of it. I was part of it. So my mind says, “That was you. You poisoned it. Everything you touched went bad.”

Even when someone says, “You’re not to blame,” I don’t feel relieved. I almost feel like they just don’t know the whole truth, or they’re being kind because they don’t want to say what I already know. And then I think, if all that damage came from me, then whatever happens to me after is just what I deserve. So yes… people tell me I’m not actually to blame, but I still feel like I am. Completely.
Are you completely certain that what happened was your fault, even though other people tell you it wasn’t?

Yes… I mean, that’s the part that scares me, because I know people keep telling me it wasn’t my fault. They say it wasn’t that simple, that there were other things going on, that I’m taking too much on myself. And I can hear them saying it, I really can. I don’t want to act like I don’t understand the words.

But inside, I feel certain. Completely certain, most of the time. Like if I trace it all back, it keeps ending with me. My husband got worse, and I keep thinking, “That happened because of me.” The crew lost work, and I think, “That was because I was involved.” Clients’ homes got messed up, and my mind just goes, “Of course they did, because you touched it.”

It’s like there’s this stain on me, or like I poisoned everything I got near. I know that sounds dramatic, but that’s how it feels. I don’t just feel sad about it — I feel guilty, like I caused damage and now whatever happens to me is deserved. Even when someone tries to reassure me, it doesn’t really reach the part of me that already knows I’m the reason it all went bad.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Yes. I have been, and I hate saying that because it makes me sound… I don’t know. But yes.

It’s usually a man’s voice. Not like my own thoughts exactly, not like when you remember something someone said. It sounds like it’s coming from behind me, clear enough that I turn around. It’s happened at job sites, when I’m working or looking over something, and it’s happened in my kitchen too, when I’m just standing there doing something normal.

He’ll say things like, “You missed it,” or, “Everyone knows.” Short things. Not a whole conversation most of the time, but it cuts through everything, like someone is standing right behind my shoulder. And I’ll turn around expecting to see a guy there, or someone from the crew, or my husband, or just… someone. But nobody’s there.

And then I feel stupid and scared at the same time, because it was so clear. It isn’t like a vague feeling. It’s not just worry. I hear it like sound, like a voice in the room. Sometimes I’ll check the hallway or look around the kitchen because I’m sure someone must have said it. But there’s no one.
Before this past year, was there ever a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks and had thoughts like this or heard voices?

No, not before this past year… or, I guess, before this whole stretch started. It’s been about a year and five months now, since my husband hurt his back and became mostly stuck at home. That’s when everything really started changing for me.

Before that, I had hard times, I mean everybody does, and I’d get sad or stressed, especially with work and money and the physical strain of the job, but it wasn’t like this. It wasn’t this nearly every day kind of thing, and I wasn’t having thoughts like this, and I wasn’t hearing voices.

This all feels tied to that point — his injury, him being mostly housebound, and then everything after that. So… about a year and five months. That’s how long it’s been going on.

I don’t have a clear memory of a specific stretch where I can say, yes, that was definitely two weeks straight of being depressed nearly every day. It may have happened in some way, but I don’t want to say yes if I’m just filling in the blanks.

So I guess my answer is… I don’t know. Nothing specific is coming to mind from before this past year that I can confidently point to.

doctor.question: Is the stress from your husband’s injury still going on in your life now?

patient.answer:
Yes. It’s still going on. It’s been… about a year and five months now, I think, since my husband hurt his back and became mostly stuck at home. I don’t know, sometimes I lose track because it all kind of blends together, but it’s definitely not over.

It’s not like it was just an accident and then things went back to normal. His injury changed the way things run every day, and that stress is still just part of the house now. So yes, it’s ongoing — it’s been going on since then.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depression is better explained as an adjustment disorder by asking if mood symptoms are tied specifically to the ongoing stressor rather than pervasive across contexts.
doctor.question: When you have a day that feels a little lighter, is it usually because something about your husband’s situation eases up?

target_item.reason: The question is asking whether mood improves when the ongoing stressor of the husband’s situation eases, which is not directly covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can connect it that directly. I mean… sometimes if something with him is calmer that day, maybe the house feels a little less tight, if that makes sense. But I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear pattern where I think, “Oh, today feels lighter because his situation eased up.”

Some days feel a little better and I can’t really tell why. It might be the mood in the house, or maybe I slept differently, or maybe I just got through the morning without as much pressure building up. And other days, even if nothing new is happening with him, I still feel weighed down by it, like it’s just there in the background.

So I guess… maybe sometimes, but I wouldn’t want to say that’s usually the reason. I haven’t really tracked it that closely.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depression includes mood reactivity to positive events, which helps distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder with depressed mood/mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
doctor.question: When something genuinely good happens, does your mood lift, even briefly?

target_item.reason: The question asks about mood reactivity—whether the patient’s mood lifts in response to genuinely positive events—which is not specifically covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure. I mean, I think it depends what you mean by “lift.” If something good happens, I can recognize that it’s good, like I know I should feel glad about it, and sometimes there is a little… I don’t know, a little break in the heaviness maybe.

But I don’t know if I’d call it my whole mood lifting. Sometimes it’s more like I smile or I say, “That’s good,” but inside it still feels kind of flat or weighed down. Other times maybe I do feel lighter for a short bit, but then it fades pretty fast and I’m back to the same place.

So I guess my honest answer is maybe briefly sometimes, but I haven’t really paid close enough attention to say it clearly. It’s not like I reliably bounce up when something good happens.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the depression is tied specifically to the ongoing stressor or occurs independently, to distinguish adjustment disorder with depressed mood from a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Even on days when nothing stressful is happening with your husband, do you still feel depressed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: For most of the time since this started, the guilt, exhaustion, loss of interest, and thoughts about death have been there, even if some weeks were less crushing than others.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether depressive symptoms persist even when the husband-related stressor is absent, which most directly concerns the persistence and predominance of the depressive episode over time rather than being only stress-reactive.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I mean, I wish I could say it only happens when something with him is bad that day, because then at least it would make sense, like there’s a direct reason right in front of me. But even on days when there isn’t some new crisis or he’s not needing as much or the house is quieter, I still feel it.

For most of the time since all this started, it’s just been there. The guilt is there, like I’m failing somehow or not doing enough. The exhaustion is there even when the day itself isn’t especially stressful. I still don’t really feel interested in things the way I used to, even if there’s technically time or space to do something. And… the thoughts about death, those have been there too. Not every single second, and some weeks are less crushing than others, but they don’t just disappear because that particular day is calmer.

So yes, even when nothing big is happening with my husband, I still feel depressed. It’s more like the stress made everything worse, but the depression doesn’t turn off just because the stress is quiet for a little while.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the current depressive episode includes mood-congruent psychotic guilt/delusional beliefs, which would strongly support major depressive disorder over adjustment disorder and clarify severity.
doctor.question: Do you believe you truly deserve to die as punishment for what you’ve done?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep thinking it would be better if I didn't wake up, and sometimes I feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to my family and my crew.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about believing death is deserved as punishment, which concerns suicidal/death thoughts rather than general guilt alone.

patient.answer:
I… that’s hard to say out loud. Part of me knows, or at least I’m supposed to know, that nobody should be thinking of death as some kind of punishment. But when I’m really down in it, yes, it feels like that. It feels like maybe it would be fair, like if I didn’t wake up, that would be what I deserve for what I’ve done to my family and my crew.

That’s actually part of why I came in, because those thoughts keep coming back. It’s not just “I’m tired” in a normal way. It’s more like I keep thinking it would be better if I didn’t wake up, like everyone would be spared me or the damage I’ve caused. And then I feel ashamed even saying that, because I know how awful that sounds.

I don’t know if I believe it every minute, but when the guilt gets really loud, dying feels like the punishment that would match it. Like that would settle the account somehow. And I know that probably doesn’t make sense from the outside, but inside it can feel very real.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has ever been a past major depressive episode to distinguish single-episode major depression from recurrent major depression.
doctor.question: Before this past year, was there ever a time when you lost interest or pleasure in most things for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to paint, cook big meals, run before jobs, and show up for theater rehearsals, but now those things feel like chores from somebody else's life and I don't care if I miss them.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about loss of interest or pleasure in most things for at least two weeks.

patient.answer:
Before this past year… no, not like this. I mean, I’ve had tired stretches before, like anybody, where I didn’t feel like doing much for a few days, or I’d skip something because work ran me into the ground. But I still had things that felt like mine.

I used to paint. Not professionally or anything, but I’d get lost in it for hours. And I liked cooking big meals, especially if people were coming over or even just making too much food because it felt good to make something. I used to run before jobs sometimes, even if it was early and I complained about it, because it cleared my head. And theater rehearsals… I’d show up for those. I cared about being there, about the lines and the people and the whole thing.

Now all of that feels like chores from somebody else’s life. Like I can remember that I used to care, but I don’t feel connected to it. If I miss rehearsal or don’t paint or don’t cook, there’s not even much disappointment, just this blankness, like, “Okay, I didn’t do it.” So before this past year, I don’t think I had a two-week period where most things lost their pleasure like that. This feels different.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode includes psychotic features by clarifying if the patient's guilt-based belief is delusional, which helps distinguish major depressive disorder from bipolar or adjustment disorder and affects severity/specification.
doctor.question: Do you believe you actually caused your husband’s injury?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I'm the reason my husband got worse, the crew lost work, and clients' homes got messed up, like I poisoned everything I touched and deserve whatever happens to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether I believe I caused my husband's injury, which directly concerns excessive guilt and self-blame.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t know how to answer that in a clean way. If you mean, do I know for a fact that I directly caused it, like with my own hands or because I chose one exact thing that made it happen… I don’t know. I can’t prove that. But inside, it feels like yes. It feels like I’m the reason he got worse.

I keep going back over everything, every decision, every job, every time I pushed or didn’t push, every time I was distracted or tired or thought something would be fine. And it all turns into this one conclusion in my head, that if I had been different, better, more careful, less selfish, then maybe he wouldn’t have gotten hurt or maybe he wouldn’t have gotten worse after. It’s like I infected the whole situation somehow.

And it’s not just him. I keep thinking the crew lost work because of me, and the clients’ homes got messed up because of me, and everything I touched turned bad. Like I poisoned it. That’s the phrase that keeps coming up in my head, like I poisoned everything I touched. So when you ask if I believe I caused his injury… I guess I believe I caused the damage around it, even if I can’t explain it in a way that would make sense to someone else.

And then it feels like whatever happens to me after that, I deserve it. Like if people are angry, if things fall apart, if I lose everything, that’s just the consequence of what I did. It feels hard to separate what actually happened from what I feel responsible for, because the guilt just swallows the whole thing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the guilt has reached delusional intensity, which would support major depressive disorder with psychotic features over adjustment disorder or bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Do you believe, as a fact, that you poisoned everything you touched?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I'm the reason my husband got worse, the crew lost work, and clients' homes got messed up, like I poisoned everything I touched and deserve whatever happens to me.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about the patient's guilt-based belief that she 'poisoned everything' and caused harm, which matches the worthlessness/excessive guilt symptom profile.

patient.answer:
As a fact… I mean, I know how that sounds. If you’re asking me like, could someone test it or prove it, no, I don’t think there’s some literal poison on my hands or anything like that. I know that doesn’t make sense in that kind of way.

But it feels true. That’s the problem. It feels like everything I was near got ruined because of me. My husband got worse, and I keep thinking there had to be something I did or didn’t do that made that happen. The crew lost work, and I hear myself saying, “That’s because of me.” Clients’ homes got messed up, and even if there are a hundred other reasons something went wrong, my mind goes straight to, “You touched it, you were involved, so of course it went bad.”

So do I believe it as a fact? I don’t know. Maybe not in the way you mean “fact.” But when I’m sitting alone with it, it doesn’t feel like just a thought. It feels like the truth about me, like I damage things by being part of them. And then whatever happens to me after that feels deserved. Like if everything falls apart, that’s just what should happen because I caused it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether her excessive guilt has reached delusional intensity, which would support major depressive disorder with psychotic features over adjustment disorder or bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Has anyone else told you that you are not actually to blame for what happened, but you still feel completely certain that you are?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I'm the reason my husband got worse, the crew lost work, and clients' homes got messed up, like I poisoned everything I touched and deserve whatever happens to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent certainty of being to blame despite others saying otherwise, which directly concerns excessive or possibly delusional guilt.

patient.answer:
Yes. People have said that to me. My husband has, in his way, and other people too, like they’ll say, “You couldn’t have known,” or “That wasn’t on you,” or “There were other reasons things went wrong.” They try to explain it like it was circumstances, or bad luck, or decisions other people made, not something I caused.

And I hear them. I can repeat the words back. I understand, in my head, what they’re trying to tell me. But it doesn’t land. It’s like there’s this wall between what they say and what I feel is true.

Because I still keep coming back to the same thing: my husband got worse, the crew lost work, clients’ homes got messed up, and I was right there in the middle of it. I was part of it. So my mind says, “That was you. You poisoned it. Everything you touched went bad.”

Even when someone says, “You’re not to blame,” I don’t feel relieved. I almost feel like they just don’t know the whole truth, or they’re being kind because they don’t want to say what I already know. And then I think, if all that damage came from me, then whatever happens to me after is just what I deserve. So yes… people tell me I’m not actually to blame, but I still feel like I am. Completely.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the guilt belief is delusional/held with fixed certainty, which best separates major depressive episode with psychotic features from nonpsychotic depression/adjustment disorder and helps distinguish from bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Are you completely certain that what happened was your fault, even though other people tell you it wasn’t?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I'm the reason my husband got worse, the crew lost work, and clients' homes got messed up, like I poisoned everything I touched and deserve whatever happens to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent certainty that I am at fault despite others saying I am not, which directly matches excessive or delusional guilt and self-blame.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, that’s the part that scares me, because I know people keep telling me it wasn’t my fault. They say it wasn’t that simple, that there were other things going on, that I’m taking too much on myself. And I can hear them saying it, I really can. I don’t want to act like I don’t understand the words.

But inside, I feel certain. Completely certain, most of the time. Like if I trace it all back, it keeps ending with me. My husband got worse, and I keep thinking, “That happened because of me.” The crew lost work, and I think, “That was because I was involved.” Clients’ homes got messed up, and my mind just goes, “Of course they did, because you touched it.”

It’s like there’s this stain on me, or like I poisoned everything I got near. I know that sounds dramatic, but that’s how it feels. I don’t just feel sad about it — I feel guilty, like I caused damage and now whatever happens to me is deserved. Even when someone tries to reassure me, it doesn’t really reach the part of me that already knows I’m the reason it all went bad.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has other psychotic symptoms beyond mood-congruent guilt delusions, which would support major depressive disorder with psychotic features over nonpsychotic depression or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I hear a man's voice from behind me at job sites or in my kitchen saying things like, 'You missed it' or 'Everyone knows,' clear as if someone is standing there, but when I turn around nobody's there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking directly about hearing voices when no one is present, which matches hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Yes. I have been, and I hate saying that because it makes me sound… I don’t know. But yes.

It’s usually a man’s voice. Not like my own thoughts exactly, not like when you remember something someone said. It sounds like it’s coming from behind me, clear enough that I turn around. It’s happened at job sites, when I’m working or looking over something, and it’s happened in my kitchen too, when I’m just standing there doing something normal.

He’ll say things like, “You missed it,” or, “Everyone knows.” Short things. Not a whole conversation most of the time, but it cuts through everything, like someone is standing right behind my shoulder. And I’ll turn around expecting to see a guy there, or someone from the crew, or my husband, or just… someone. But nobody’s there.

And then I feel stupid and scared at the same time, because it was so clear. It isn’t like a vague feeling. It’s not just worry. I hear it like sound, like a voice in the room. Sometimes I’ll check the hallway or look around the kitchen because I’m sure someone must have said it. But there’s no one.
